sec.title: Background
sec.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) pose a significant challenge as a highly aggressive and currently incurable form of pediatric brain cancer, necessitating the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Omacetaxine, an FDA-approved protein synthesis inhibitor for treating certain hematological malignancies, was investigated for its potential antitumor effects against preclinical DIPG models.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We employed primary DIPG cultures to study omacetaxine’s cytotoxicity and its impact on colony formation. Annexin V staining and flow cytometry assessed apoptosis. Wound healing assays evaluated migration, while western blotting determined inhibition of oncogenic proteins. We tested omacetaxine’s therapeutic efficacy in an orthotopic DIPG model and assessed brain penetration using mass spectrometry.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We found a pronounced cytotoxic activity of omacetaxine against DIPG neurospheres, with low IC50 values of approximately 20 nM. Omacetaxine exerted its anti-proliferative effect by inhibiting protein synthesis and the induction of apoptotic pathways, evidenced by significant elevated levels of cleaved caspase 3 and cleaved PARP, both key markers of apoptosis. Omacetaxine effectively targeted oncogenic players such as PDGFRα and PI3K without additional effects on the mTOR signaling pathway. Furthermore, our study revealed the inhibitory effects of omacetaxine on cell migration, and a significant reduction in integrin/FAK signaling, which plays a crucial role in tumor progression and metastasis.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Despite these promising in vitro effects, omacetaxine’s efficacy in an orthotopic DIPG model was limited due to inadequate penetration across the blood-brain barrier. As such, further research and advancements are crucial to improve the drug’s brain penetration, thus enhancing its overall therapeutic potential.
Keywords: IPG, integrin signaling, omacetaxine, PDGFRα/PI3K, protein synthesis inhibitor
Collection date 2024 Jan-Dec.

list-item.p: Omacetaxine is cytotoxic to DIPG neurospheres, inhibiting protein synthesis and inducing apoptosis.
It targets key oncogenic proteins and reduces cell migration.
Omacetaxine displays limited efficacy in an orthotopic DIPG model due to poor brain penetration.

boxed-text.p: This study explores the potential of omacetaxine as a novel therapeutic approach for DIPG a highly aggressive and currently incurable pediatric brain cancer. Through in-depth mechanistic investigations, the study elucidates how omacetaxine exerts cytotoxic effects by inhibiting protein synthesis, inducing apoptosis, and targeting key oncogenic proteins, offering insights for the development of targeted DIPG therapies. Notably, the study identifies a limitation in omacetaxine’s poor blood-brain barrier penetration in an orthotopic DIPG model, prompting further research to enhance drug delivery strategies.

body.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPG) are highly malignant brain tumors primarily affecting children.1 Current treatment options are limited, with conventional radiotherapy being the only available approach that partially improves neurological function and extends survival, but is not curative.2 Despite numerous clinical trials with complex treatment strategies, the prognosis for DIPG remains poor, with most children succumbing to the disease within 1–2 years of diagnosis. The infiltrative and inaccessible nature of the tumor precludes surgical removal, necessitating the urgent exploration of novel chemotherapeutic treatment.3,4 Encouragingly, the discovery of key driver mutations, such as histone H3K27M, in approximately 80% of DIPG cases, as well as other genomic alterations, including TP53, ACVR1, PI3K mutations, and PDGFRα amplification, has renewed hope for the development of targeted therapies for this aggressive disease.5–8 However, even targeting these aberrations has been proven difficult due to limited drug penetration influenced by an intact blood-brain barrier (BBB), demanding the exploration of innovative therapeutic approaches.9–12

Omacetaxine, an FDA-approved anticancer agent primarily used for treating chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), exerts its primary mechanism of action by inhibiting protein synthesis by targeting the A-site of the large ribosome.13–16 This inhibition impacts short-lived proteins, including the oncogenic player BCR-ABL, leading to antileukemic effects.17 Recent studies have highlighted the efficacy of combining omacetaxine with sorafenib in treating relapsed/refractory acute myeloid leukemia (AML), with antitumor efficacy through enhanced inhibition of FLT3-ITD (18) leading to encouraging patient outcomes.18

In addition to CML and AML, omacetaxine has displayed antitumor effects across various solid cancers, with the effects on protein synthesis leading to the inhibition of a wide range of signaling pathways. Multiple studies have documented activity in solid malignancies, including lung, breast, bladder, hepatocellular carcinoma, and gastrointestinal cancers.19–24 In gastrointestinal tumors, omacetaxine downregulates oncoproteins such as KIT, while in hepatocellular carcinoma, it inhibits PLK1.19,20 In breast cancer, its cytotoxic effects are mediated through modulating the miR-18a-3p-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway.23 In lung cancer, omacetaxine directly interacts with and inhibits the calcium-activated chloride channel TMEM16A.22 Additionally, omacetaxine’s antitumor effects in bladder cancer have been attributed to its impact on the integrin/FAK/Src axis.24

Some early data are suggesting that omacetaxine has promising preclinical activity in CNS tumors. One study showed activity in glioblastoma in vitro and in zebrafish models, and another in meningioma using subcutaneous xenografts xenograft models.25,26 In glioblastoma, its antitumor effects were attributed to the inhibition of cell migration and evasion mediated by the PDGFRα/Rho/ROCK axis.25 Notably, its activity has not yet been assessed in orthotopic brain tumor mouse models. Considering the highly infiltrative nature of pediatric gliomas like DIPG and the activity of omacetaxine against signaling pathways that contribute to its oncogenesis, we aimed to investigate the anticancer potential and mechanism of action of omacetaxine in this devastating pediatric brainstem tumor.

sec.title: Cell Culture and Reagents
sec.p: Patient-derived DIPG cultures HSJD-DIPG007, SU-DIPGVI, and VUMC-DIPG10 were generously provided by collaborators at Stanford University (USA) and St John of Hope Hospital (Spain), respectively. DIPG cultures RA055 and P002306, along with normal astrocytes (P000302), were derived from biopsy specimens obtained from patients participating in the Zero Childhood Cancer precision medicine program (ZERO). These DIPG cultures were cultivated using a combination of DMEM/F12 and Neurobasal media (in a 1:1 ratio), supplemented with heparin, B27, human epidermal growth factor (EGF), human fibroblast growth factor (FGF), platelet-derived growth factor-AA (PDGF-AA), platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB), HEPES, non-essential amino acids, antibiotic/antimycotic agents, pyruvate, and glutamax. All cells were maintained under optimal conditions at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% carbon dioxide (CO2). The P000302 astrocytes were cultured using the same media as the DIPG cultures but supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS). All cultures have undergone authentication by STR profiling.

sec.title: Cell Viability Assay
sec.p: DIPG cells and normal brain cells (P000302) were seeded in 96-well plates at densities of 2000–3000 cells per 100 μl of culture media. The cells were then incubated for 72 h to allow neurospheres to form or establish adherent monolayers. After this initial incubation period, the cells were treated with various concentrations of omacetaxine for an additional 72 h. Cell viability was assessed using the resazurin dye reduction assay, which measures the metabolic activity of the cells and serves as an indirect indicator of cell viability. The reduction of resazurin dye is indicative of active cell metabolism. To determine the IC50 values representing the drug concentrations required to inhibit 50% of cell growth, nonlinear regression analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, California, USA).

sec.title: Clonogenic Assay
sec.p: Long-term clonogenic assays were employed to assess the effect of omacetaxine on the clonogenic potential of DIPG cells. 24-well plates were coated initially with a media mixture containing 0.5% soft agar. Following a 24-h incubation, cell suspensions in media supplemented with 0.33% agar and either the drugs of interest or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a vehicle control were added to the bottom agar layer. Approximately 500–1000 cells were seeded per well to facilitate colony formation, and the plates were then incubated in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2 at 37°C for 2–3 weeks. After the incubation period, the formed colonies were stained with a 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) solution at a concentration of 5 mg/ml. The stained colonies were subsequently visualized and quantified using ImageJ software, allowing for accurate colony counting and analysis.

sec.title: Apoptosis Assays
sec.p: Flow cytometric analysis was conducted using Annexin V and propidium iodide staining to assess omacetaxine’s effect on programmed cell death. RA055 DIPG cells were plated on laminin-coated plates at a density of 300 000 cells per 3 ml of culture media and incubated for 24 h. Subsequently, the cells were treated with increasing concentrations of omacetaxine for 24 h. After treatment, the cells were stained with 2 µl of Annexin V-FITC and/or propidium iodide according to the manufacturer’s instructions (BD Biosciences). The staining was performed in the dark for 15 min. Following the staining process, the samples were immediately analyzed using a BD FACs Canto analyzer (BD Biosciences), with a collection of 10 000 events for each sample.

sec.title: Migration Assay
sec.p: To evaluate the impact of omacetaxine on the migratory ability of DIPG cells, a wound healing assay was conducted. Two-well silicone inserts (Ibidi, Cat. No: 80209) were positioned in 12-well plates, creating a gap between the cells. Subsequently, 1 × 105 DIPG cells with 5% fetal calf serum were seeded on either side of the inserts. After 24 h of incubation, the inserts were gently removed using sterile forceps, and omacetaxine was introduced into the wells at the specified dose. Images of the wound gap were captured at 0 h, 6 h, 24 h, and 30 h time points. The acquired images were analyzed using ImageJ Software (ImageJ, Maryland, USA) to quantify and assess changes in wound closure over time.

sec.title: Protein Synthesis Assay
sec.p: RA055 cells were seeded at a cell density of 20 000 cells/well in laminin-coated Nunc™ Lab-Tek™ II 8-well chamber slides (ThermoFisher Scientific) and cultured for 24 h. Cells were then treated for 4 h with omacetaxine at 0, 0.1, 1, and 10 µM, and cycloheximide (CHX) at 100 µg/ml as a positive control. Protein synthesis in cells was evaluated by Click-iT® Plus OPP Alexa Fluor® 488 Protein Synthesis Assay (ThermoFisher Scientific) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, after the drug treatment, cells were treated with puromycin at the concentration of 20 µM for 30 min prior to fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde and permeabilization in 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS. Cells untreated with omacetaxine and puromycin were also included as a negative control. Cells were stained for puromycin incorporation using Alexa Fluor 488 and for nucleus staining using HCS NuclearMask™ Blue Stain in the kit. Fluorescent images were then acquired using the Olympus Slideview VS200 (Olympus Life Science Solution, Australia) and analyzed using QuPath software. Fluorescence intensity was measured for quantification using ImageJ with the same setting for all images.

sec.title: Western Blot Analysis
sec.p: RA055 DIPG cells were seeded at a density of 300 000 cells per 3 ml of culture media onto laminin-coated plates and allowed to adhere for up to 48 h. Subsequently, the cells were treated with two different concentrations of omacetaxine, namely 1 and 10 μM, with or without the combination of 50 μM caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK (Selleck Chemicals) for 24 h. Cells were also treated with cycloheximide at 10 and 100 μg/ml for 24 h. Following the treatment, the cells were lysed using RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The protein concentration in the lysates was quantified using the Pierce BCA Analysis Kit following the manufacturer’s instructions. A total of 20 μg of protein was then mixed with Laemmli loading buffer containing 10% DTT (Bio-Rad) and incubated at 95˚C for 5 min to denature the proteins. Subsequently, electrophoresis was conducted at 100 V for 1–1.5 h to separate the proteins based on their molecular weight. The separated proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (BioRad) at 100 V for 1 h. To prevent non-specific binding, the membranes were blocked using a solution of 5% skim milk in tri-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST). The membranes were then incubated overnight at 4˚C with primary antibodies, which were diluted in a solution of 5% bovine serum albumin or 5% nonfat milk in TBST at 1:1000 dilution. All rabbit monoclonal primary antibodies (anti-human) were purchased from Cell Signaling Technologies (CST) as follows: PARP (#9532), cleaved PARP (#5625), Caspase 3 (#9662), cleaved Caspase 3 (#9664), phospho-H2A.X (#9718), phospho-PDGFRα (Tyr754) (#2992), PDGFRα (#3164), phospho-PI3K p85 (Tyr458)/p55 (Tyr199) (#4228), PI3K p85 (#4257), phospho-Akt (Ser473) (#4058), Akt (#9272), phospho-mTOR (Ser2448) (#2971), mTOR (#2972), Integrin αV (#4711), Integrin α4 (#8440), Integrin α5 (#4705), Integrin β1 (#9699), Integrin β3 (#13166), Integrin β4 (#14803), Integrin β5 (#3629), phospho-FAK (Tyr397) (#8556), FAK (#3285), phospho-Src (Tyr527) (#2105), Src (#2109), phospho-Talin (Ser425) (#5426), Talin-1 (#4021), Paxillin (#12065), Tensin 2 (#11990), Vinculin (#4650), α-Actinin (#6487), α-Tubulin (#2144), β3-Tubulin (#5568), tri-methyl-Histone H3 (Lys27) (#9733), acetyl-Histone H3 (Lys27) (#8173), Histone H3 (#9717), β-Actin (#8457) and GAPDH (#5174). After the overnight incubation, the membranes were washed three times with TBST to remove any unbound primary antibodies. Subsequently, the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) in TBST for 1 h at room temperature. The membrane protein bands were visualized using the Enhanced Chemiluminescence (ECL) detection kit (ThermoFisher Scientific). Images of protein bands were captured using ChemiDoc™ Touch Imaging System (Bio-Rad).and densitometry of protein bands was analyzed using Image J.

sec.title: In vivo Experiments
sec.p: All animal experiments were strictly adhered to the guidelines set by the Animal Care and Ethics Committee of the University of New South Wales and the Australian Code of Practice for Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes using the approved protocol 22/46B. Animals were housed in a controlled environment with a 12-h light/dark cycle, maintaining optimal temperature conditions. DIPG orthotopic models were developed as per previously established protocol.27 Briefly, female Balb c/nude mice (-6 weeks old, obtained from the Animal Resources Centre, Perth, Australia) were subjected to stereotactic injection of 200,000 RA055 cells suspended in 2 µl of matrigel into the fourth ventricle/pons region. Throughout the experimental period, all animals were monitored daily for any signs of weight loss and neurological symptoms that may arise from omacetaxine treatments or tumor engraftment. In cases where symptoms such as ataxia, circling, head tilting, or weight loss exceeding 20% of the original body weight were observed, the mice were humanely euthanized. Treatment with omacetaxine was initiated three weeks after the intracranial injection of DIPG cells. The animals were treated intraperitoneally with either the vehicle or omacetaxine at a dosage of 1 mg/kg/day, administered three days per week for three weeks (amounting to a total of 15 treatments). Two to three hours following the last 15th treatment, a subset of three animals from each group were humanely euthanized for immunohistochemical analyses and six mice from each group for pharmacokinetic study.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Brain tissue from the vehicle and omacetaxine-treated animals was fixed using 10% formalin and subsequently embedded in paraffin. Thin sections of 5 μM were cut from the embedded tissues and mounted on Superfrost slides. The slides were then dried in a 60°C oven for 1 h and subjected to deparaffinization using xylene for 20 min. The slides were rehydrated through sequential incubation in 100%, 90%, and 70% ethanol solutions, followed by MilliQ water. For antigen retrieval, the slides were immersed in 100 mM tri-sodium citrate buffer at pH 6 and subjected to heat treatment. The slides were heated for 20 min, with a cooling interval of 10 min following every 5 min of heating. This process facilitated the retrieval of antigens for subsequent immunostaining. The endogenous peroxidases were inactivated by immersing the slides in a 3% hydrogen peroxide solution to block non-specific binding of immunoglobulins. Subsequently, the slides were treated with a blocking solution consisting of 2.5% bovine serum albumin, 2.5% fetal calf serum, and 0.2% Triton-X for 1 h at room temperature. Next, the slides were incubated with primary antibodies Ki67 (#RM-9106, ThermoFisher Scientific) and cleaved PARP (CST#5625) at 4°C overnight. Following the incubation with primary antibodies, the slides were incubated with appropriate secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Finally, the slides were washed with MilliQ water and subjected to dehydration using sequential incubations in 70%, 90%, and 100% ethanol solutions for mounting with coverslips. Images were acquired using Olympus Slideview SV200 (Olympus, Australia) and analyzed using QuPath-0.4.3. Positive staining cells with Ki67 and cleaved-PARP were counted and analyzed using ImageJ.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic Analysis
sec.p: Omacetaxine in mouse brain was analyzed using ultra high-performance liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Mouse brains were snap-frozen approximately 3 h after the 15th intraperitoneal administration of omacetaxine during a 3-week treatment period. Two portions of brain tissue, the frontal lobe, and cerebellum together with the brainstem, were homogenized in chilled methanol containing 0.1% formic acid [1:9 ratio (w/v), ie, 9 µl solvent per mg tissue] using a homogenizer (OMNI International, Kennesaw, GA) with OMNI disposable probes. Tissue homogenates were vortexed for 30 min at 4°C and centrifuged at 17 000g for 15 min at 4°C. The same volume of supernatant from each sample was transferred into a 1 ml microcentrifuge tube (Eppendorf) and reduced to dryness overnight in a SpeedVac Vacuum Concentrator (ThermoFisher Scientific). The residue in each tube was resuspended in methanol containing 0.1% formic acid to a concentration 10× higher than the original solution. LC-MS/MS was performed on a ThermoFisher U3000 System with a Waters BEH C18 2.1 × 50 mm UHPLC column and a Quantum Access mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific). In addition to experimental samples, mouse brain tissue spiked with different known amounts of omacetaxine was extracted and analyzed as a quality control. Data were processed and chromatograms integrated automatically using XCalibur software and Microsoft Excel.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9 software to determine the significance of the results. For in vitro experiments and immunohistochemistry analyses, one-way ANOVA was applied. The Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test assessed survival analyses of orthotopic xenografts. To analyze images, ImageJ software (ImageJ, Maryland, USA) was utilized for quantitative measurements and data extraction. A threshold of P < .05 was set as the statistical significance level to determine the findings’ significance.

sec.title: Cytotoxic Efficacy of Omacetaxine in DIPG Primary Cultures
sec.p: Omacetaxine has been previously studied for its cytotoxic activity in various cancer models,25 but its effect on pediatric brain tumors such as DIPG remains unexplored. We used the Alamar Blue proliferation assay to determine the cytotoxic efficacy of omacetaxine following a 72 h treatment against a panel of DIPG cultures that form neurospheres. These cultures represent the common H3K27M mutant subtype (HSJD-DIPG007, P002306, RA055, SU-DIPGVI) as well as the H3K27 wild type (VUMC-DIPG10). Results indicated that all five DIPG cultures responded similarly to omacetaxine, exhibiting low IC50 concentrations ranging from approximately 20–30 nM following a 72 h treatment period (Figure 1A).

caption.p: Omacetaxine reduces the proliferation and colony formation of DIPG cells. (A) Cytotoxic efficacy of omacetaxine across a panel of DIPG cells and normal astrocytes (P000302). Cells were treated with omacetaxine for 72 h and assessed for proliferation by Alamar Blue assay. Treated cells were compared to the control and presented as average % viability ±SEM. Experiments were performed three times, with each time N = 6–8; (B, C) Omacetaxine reduces colony formation along a range of concentrations in RA055 and HSJD-DIPG007 cultures, respectively. DIPG colonies were stained with MTT approximately 2–3 weeks upon formation of colonies. Data are presented as the average % of colony formation ±SEM compared to untreated colonies. Each experiment was performed twice, with each time. N = 6–8 *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < .0001.

sec.p: Additionally, we evaluated the impact of omacetaxine in a normal astrocyte culture (P000302) derived from a pediatric patient. These cells demonstrated lower sensitivity to omacetaxine, with an IC50 value nearly ten times higher at 200 nM (Figure 1A). To further investigate the antitumor effect of omacetaxine, we performed an anchorage-dependent colony-forming assay in two H3K27M primary cultures. We found that omacetaxine potently inhibited colony formation in both DIPG cultures. Notably, this effect was observed at very low nanomolar concentrations of omacetaxine (Figure 1B and C).

sec.title: Omacetaxine Induces Apoptotic Cell Death
sec.p: We next employed two experimental approaches to investigate the potential of omacetaxine enhancing apoptotic cell death in DIPG cells. Flow cytometric analysis of cells treated with increasing concentrations of omacetaxine (1 and 10 µM) for a shorter treatment period of 24 h revealed significantly higher levels of apoptotic cell death, as indicated by annexin-FITC and propidium iodide staining (Figure 2A). Furthermore, western blotting experiments demonstrated significantly higher levels of DNA damage marker p-H2AX and the apoptosis markers, cleaved PARP, and cleaved caspase 3 in DIPG cells treated with omacetaxine for 24 h (Figure 2B, Supplementary Figure 1A). Furthermore, omacetaxine-induced apoptosis and DNA damage could be rescued by pan caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK through inhibition of cleaved caspase 3, cleaved PARP as well as p-H2AX (Supplementary Figure 1B–D). These findings strongly support the notion that omacetaxine induces a cytotoxic response through the induction of apoptosis in DIPG cultures. Given the apoptotic effects observed following 24 h treatment at these concentrations, further mechanistic analysis performed below was performed using this treatment period and concentrations.

caption.p: Omacetaxine induces apoptotic cell death in DIPG cells. (A) Flow cytometric analysis of RA055 cells treated with increasing concentrations of omacetaxine for 24 h. Cells were stained with Annexin-FITC and propidium iodide and were analyzed with FACS Canto. Data presented is an average of % of early and late apoptotic cells. The experiment was performed three times, each time N = 3. (B) Western blotting analysis of RA055 cells treated with 1 µM and 10 µM of omacetaxine for 24 h and analyzed for the levels of proteins involved in apoptosis (cleaved PARP and cleaved Caspase 3) and DNA damage (phospho-H2AX). Significantly higher levels of cleaved PARP, cleaved Caspase 3, and p-H2AX were observed in the treated samples (N = 3). ***P < .001, ****P < .0001.

sec.title: Omacetaxine Inhibits Protein Synthesis and Oncogenic Players
sec.p: Omacetaxine’s key mechanism of action has been attributed to the inhibition of protein synthesis. To validate this effect specifically in DIPG cells, we assessed puromycin incorporation into the nascent protein chains in RA055 DIPG cells subjected to increasing concentrations of omacetaxine for 24 h. Our findings revealed that untreated cells exhibited normal puromycin incorporation, while DIPG cells treated with increasing doses of omacetaxine demonstrated a significant reduction in protein synthesis, in line with the positive control group treated with cycloheximide (Figure 3A and B).

caption.p: Omacetaxine inhibits the synthesis of oncogenic proteins. (A) Representative images of RA055 cells treated with various concentrations of omacetaxine for 4 h and assessed for the inhibition of global protein synthesis using puromycin incorporation. cycloheximide (100 gµ/ml) was used as a positive control, whereas the absence of puromycin was used as a negative control. Scale bar indicates 50 μM. (B) Fluorescence intensity quantification showed that the protein synthesis in RA055 cells treated with omacetaxine at 0.1, 1, and 10 µM and cycloheximide was highly significantly reduced. ****P < .0001. (C) Western blotting analysis of RA055 treated with varying concentrations of omacetaxine for 24 h and assessed for the effects on oncogenic pathway PDGFRα/PI3K/Akt/mTOR. Significantly lower levels of total and phosphorylated PDGFRα/PI3K and phospho-Akt were observed in the treated samples, whereas no effects were observed in Akt and mTOR (N = 3).

sec.p: Given that omacetaxine has been shown to inhibit global protein synthesis by impacting oncogenic players with short half-lives, we evaluated its effects on the PDGFRα/PI3K/mTOR pathway. Given the apoptotic effects observed at the concentrations of 1 and 10 µM for 24 h we performed immunoblotting analysis at this shorter treatment window. We found significantly lower levels of p-PDGFRα, total PDGFRα and p-PI3k and PI3K in omacetaxine-treated samples (1 and 10 µM) compared to untreated controls (Figure 3C; Supplementary Figure 2). Downstream p-Akt was also significantly reduced in omacetaxine-treated samples; however, total Akt, p-mTOR, and mTOR were unaffected compared to the control (Figure 3C; Supplementary Figure 2). Furthermore, we observed that omacetaxine effectively reinstated the repression on H3K27 trimethylation, a process commonly compromised by the H3K27M mutation while concurrently promoting increased acetylation (Supplementary Figure 3). These experiments confirm that omacetaxine can inhibit the synthesis of crucial oncogenic players in DIPG, including elements of the PDGFRα/PI3K/mTOR pathway, thus revealing its potential as a valuable therapeutic intervention for this disease.

sec.title: Omacetaxine Influences Cell Migration and Integrin Signaling
sec.p: In addition to its impact on oncogenic players, omacetaxine has been reported to affect migration through integrin signaling. Using the scratch wound healing assay, we observed that untreated RA055 cells displayed migratory activity over a 30-h period. Conversely, DIPG cells treated with omacetaxine exhibited reduced migration as early as 6 h after treatment initiation (Figure 4A). This effect on migration was also observed in a second primary DIPG culture, HSJD-DIPG007 (Supplementary Figure 4).

caption.p: Omacetaxine impacts the migration of DIPG cells through inhibition of the integrin/FAK/Src axis. (A) Scratch assay was performed in RA055 cells treated with 0.1 µM of omacetaxine over a period of 30 h. Omacetaxine-treated cells display a significantly reduced ability to migrate over the scratched area as early as 6 h post-treatment. Data presented are from three independent wells, with two sample images taken from each well at each time point. (B) Western blotting analysis of RA055 treated with varying concentrations of omacetaxine for 24 h and assessed for the effects on migration governed by integrin/FAK/Src signaling pathway. Significantly lower levels of all integrin proteins were observed in the omacetaxine-treated samples, along with reduced levels of phosphorylated FAK and Src. Although no changes were observed for total FAK protein levels, significantly lower levels of total Src were observed (N = 3).

sec.p: To further explore the underlying mechanisms, we conducted immunoblotting analysis on a comprehensive panel of proteins involved in integrin receptors and downstream signaling associated with cell adhesion and motility. Treatment with omacetaxine at two concentrations (1 and 10 µM) resulted in significant reductions in integrin αV, α4, and α5 as well as β1, β3, and β5, with the most pronounced effect observed on β4. Additionally, downstream signaling analysis indicated a significant reduction in phosphorylated FAK (p-FAK) while total FAK levels remained unaffected. Similarly, reduced levels of phosphorylated Src (p-Src) and total Src were also observed following omacetaxine treatment (Figure 4B, Supplementary Figure 5).

Further examination of downstream signaling processes involved in focal adhesion, assembly, and cytoskeletal reorganization revealed an increase in phospho-Talin (p-Talin) despite unchanged total levels.

Increased phosphorylation of cytoskeletal proteins associated with integrins and focal adhesion is usually implicated in integrin activation and inhibition of focal adhesion disassembly. Additionally, omacetaxine treatments resulted in a significant increase in Paxillin levels and a decrease in Tensin 2. Notably, no significant changes were observed in the protein levels of cytoskeletal proteins, including vinculin, α-actinin, tubulins α/β3, and β-actin (Supplementary Figure 6A and B). These findings collectively indicate that omacetaxine affects crucial processes involved in cell migration and integrin signaling, highlighting its potential as a modulator of the invasive potential of DIPG cells.

To validate that the impact of omacetaxine on oncogenic players such as PI3K/AKT/mTOR and integrin signaling can be reproduced by another protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide, we conducted in vitro cytotoxicity assays and western blot analyses. Our results revealed the cytotoxic effects of cycloheximide in DIPG cells, with slightly higher IC50 values observed in two out of the three tested cell cultures, with HSJD-DIPG007 being the most sensitive (Supplementary Figure 7A). Western blot analyses, conducted at two different cycloheximide concentrations (10 and 100 µg/ml), demonstrated a significant reduction in protein levels of phospho-PI3K, total PI3, and integrin subunits α5, β1, and β3. Additionally, a noteworthy increase in apoptotic markers, including cleaved caspase 3 and cleaved PARP, was observed (Supplementary Figure 7B–D). These findings strongly suggest that protein synthesis inhibitors have the capacity to impact key oncogenic processes in DIPG cells.

sec.title: Omacetaxine Has Minimal Antitumor Efficacy and Reduced Brain Penetration
sec.p: Having demonstrated the cytotoxic potential of omacetaxine and its effect on key oncogenic players in DIPG cells, our focus shifted to evaluating its efficacy in the RA055 orthotopic animal model. This model involved the injection of DIPG cells into the fourth ventricle/pons and has been previously shown to mimic the clinical outcomes. Animals were randomized into the vehicle and omacetaxine treatment groups (1 mg/kg/day 5 days/week for 3 weeks), approximately at 2 weeks post intracranial injection. Although omacetaxine treatment was well tolerated, we observed no significant impact on animal survival compared to the vehicle control group (Figure 5A). Immunohistochemical analysis revealed similar infiltration of the Ki67-positive cells in the brainstem and cerebellum for both the vehicle and omacetaxine-treated animals. Likewise, no differences were observed in the apoptosis marker cleaved PARP (Figure 5B).

caption.p: Omacetaxine does not induce an antitumor effect in DIPG orthotopic animals due to low levels of brain penetration. (A) Survival curve of RA055 orthotopic DIPG model treated with either vehicle or omacetaxine for 3 weeks (1 mg/kg/day, 3 days/week, intraperitoneally). Each treatment cohort consisted of 12 animals. Animals were monitored for tumor engraftment based on the severity of neurological symptoms and progressive weight loss. The grey area presents the treatment duration. Omacetaxine did not enhance the survival of the animals. Median survival: vehicle = 47 days, omacetaxine: 47 days. (B) At the end of the treatment, brains were harvested from three animals in each group and assessed for effects on proliferative tumor cells stained with Ki67 and apoptotic cells stained with cleaved PARP. Omacetaxine did not affect the levels of each marker in the brain of engrafted animals. Scale bar indicates 50 μM. (C) As per efficacy and immunohistochemical analysis, pharmacokinetic analysis was assessed in animals treated with omacetaxine for the full 3-week duration. HPLC-MS analysis indicated that omacetaxine penetrates the brain in tumor free area (cortex) and tumor-engrafted area (brainstem/cerebellum), although at insufficient levels to have an antitumor effect (N = 5 per treatment).****P < .0001

sec.p: Given that an intact BBB penetration is often a limitation for the successful delivery of anticancer agents in DIPG preclinical models, we performed a pharmacokinetic analysis of omacetaxine in the brains of engrafted animals. The results indicated very low levels of omacetaxine in the isolated cortex (nonengrafted) and brainstem/cerebellum (DMG-engrafted) of 0.2 and 0.3 nM respectively, falling significantly below the reported IC50 values reported above (Figure 5C, Supplementary Figure 8). These findings suggest that despite its potent cytotoxic effect in DIPG cells, omacetaxine has poor penetration of the intact BBB in DIPG models leading to mitigation of its anti-tumor effect seen in vitro.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Pediatric DMG/DIPG tumors are the most devastating brain malignancies and despite advancements in molecular characterization, effective therapeutic options are still lacking. Therefore, new therapeutic options are urgently needed for these patients. Omacetaxine, a protein synthesis inhibitor primary used in the treatment of CML, has shown promise in preclinical studies involving various adult solid malignancies, including brain tumors.25,26 Our study provides novel insights into omacetaxine’s potential as a therapeutic agent for DIPG, demonstrating its ability to inhibit proliferation and clonogenic capacity in primary DIPG cultures while inducing apoptotic cell death at sub-micromolar concentrations.25 These concentrations fall within the range of activity documented for glioblastoma cells, although they are slightly higher compared to those reported for meningiomas (1–2 nM).25,26

Omacetaxine inhibits protein synthesis by modulating global protein translation. However, its mechanism of action has been found to be related to a pronounced effect on proteins characterized by a short half-life, including several oncoproteins such as BCR-ABL, cMYC, PLK1, PDGFRα, and STAT3.13,20,25 Recent studies have also demonstrated its effects on migration through integrin signaling inhibition in bladder cancer and glioblastoma.24,25 Interestingly our study has revealed that omacetaxine significantly impacts protein synthesis in DIPG cells, leading to alterations to the total levels and phosphorylation of PDGFRα, PI3K, and Akt without eliciting any further effects on mTOR. Additionally, we observed notable effects on multiple integrin receptors and the downstream FAK/Src axis, correlating with reduced cell migration as demonstrated in the scratch assay. This is particularly relevant given the frequent occurrence of PDGFRα/PI3K aberrations in DIPG patients, which are challenging to target effectively due to the limited penetrability of targeted agents across the BBB.28–30 Similarly, although pediatric patients with cortical and brainstem high grade gliomas have been reported to exhibit high expression levels of integrin ανβ3 receptors, the efficacy of the integrin inhibitor cilengitide has been modest at best, even at the highest administered doses.31,32 Therefore, alternative options to target these players are desirable.

While omacetaxine has demonstrated in vivo antitumor efficacy in subcutaneous xenograft brain tumor models and in zebrafish glioblastoma models, our study, the first to employ an orthotopic mouse model, revealed no improvement in the survival of animals engrafted with DIPG tumors. This lack of efficacy is most likely attributed to the minimal drug penetration in the brain at levels insufficient to elicit a cytotoxic response. Importantly, we have previously shown that the BBB remains intact in DIPG orthotopic xenografts, mimicking the clinical scenario.10 Only a limited number of studies have provided some evidence for the penetration of omacetaxine into the brains of dogs and humans, albeit with varying degrees of detection.33,34 However, subsequent Phase II studies have failed to demonstrate significant clinical activity associated with omacetaxine in patients with recurrent malignant gliomas.35 These results highlight that rigorous testing of novel agents in orthotopic models with an intact BBB is critical for a complete preclinical evaluation for tumors such as DIPG.

While our studies do not support the use of omacetaxine as a therapeutic option for DIPG, further investigations exploring alternative delivery methods would be beneficial. Strategies such as liposomal formulations to carry omacetaxine and specifically target the brain, as well as approaches inducing BBB disruption, such as microbubble ultrasound warrant exploration.36–38 Moreover, delivery approaches designed to bypass the BBB may offer a potential avenue to mitigate toxicity, particularly myelosuppression, as observed in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).39 Additionally, alternative inhibitors of the translation machinery should be evaluated preclinically in pediatric brain tumors. For instance, the rocaglate derivative CMLD010509 has demonstrated significant efficacy in multiple myeloma and could be a promising candidate worth investigating preclinically in brain tumors.40 The search for effective therapies for DIPG remains a critical priority, and ongoing research into new treatment modalities is crucial to improving outcomes for these young patients.
